basics.name: LEGO Technic references: Yoshihito Isogawa's 'The LEGO Technic Idea Book' series (Simple Machines, Wheeled Wonders, Fantastic Contraptions) and Pawel 'Sariel' Kmiec's 'The Unofficial LEGO Technic Builder's Guide' (1st and 2nd editions)
basics.url: https://sariel.pl/guide2/ (the author's page for the Builder's Guide, 2nd edition, with the full chapter list). No single web home exists for the Isogawa series; its catalogue records are at https://archive.org/details/simplemachines0000isog, https://archive.org/details/wheeledwonders0000isog and https://archive.org/details/legotechnicideab00isog (Internet Archive lending library). The publisher's pages (nostarch.com) could not be opened from this environment (HTTP 403)
basics.resource_type: book (two picture-led book series from the same publisher, No Starch Press)
basics.cost: Paid. The Isogawa Idea Books were $19.95 each when launched in 2010 (per the ROBOTMAK3RS review). The Builder's Guide 2nd edition is 'around $35/£25' (The Lego Car Blog review). All four printed books can also be borrowed free, one reader at a time, from the Internet Archive lending library with a free account
basics.license: All rights reserved (commercial books, copyright of the authors and No Starch Press; LEGO is a trademark of the LEGO Group and the books are unofficial). What this means for the encyclopedia: cite and link to them as further reading, but do not copy their photos, drawings or building instructions
basics.language: English (the No Starch editions). The Isogawa books began as Japanese books (the 'Red, Blue and Green books', mostly in Japanese text) and the English editions use very little text. The Builder's Guide is also translated: 1st edition into Finnish, German, Korean, Polish and Simplified Chinese; 2nd edition into German and Polish (list on sariel.pl/books)
basics.year: Isogawa Technic Idea Books: English editions October 2010 (library records give 2010 or 2011). Builder's Guide: 1st edition June 2012 (353 pages, 20 chapters); 2nd edition October 2016 (424 pages by the author's count, 25 chapters; Open Library records 403 pages, dated 2017). Related later Isogawa titles: The LEGO Power Functions Idea Book vols 1-2 (2015/2016) and LEGO Technic Non-Electric Models: Simple Machines (July 2021, 180 pages). No newer edition of either original series was found
basics.access_barrier: paywall (buy the book), or a free login to borrow the scanned copy for a limited time from the Internet Archive lending library (the items are marked access-restricted, i.e. controlled lending)
basics.image_license: All rights reserved, same as the text. Isogawa's photos and Sariel's rendered diagrams belong to the authors/publisher. Sariel's own website photos are also his copyright (his site warns about scam shops using stolen photos)
basics.authority_level: community or unvetted, but expert-level: both authors are well-known LEGO builders, not engineers writing to a standard. Sariel's 1st edition had a technical review by Eric Albrecht (Blakbird) and a foreword by Fernando Correia (TechnicBRICKs editor), per sariel.pl. Commercially published by No Starch Press, not peer-reviewed

coverage.covers: LEGO Technic building mechanisms, mostly transmission of motion and small machines. Isogawa vol. 1 'Simple Machines' (x + 157 pages) covers gears and power transmission: 22 sections from gears, shafts and connectors, gear combinations, gears in a turntable, gears in series, angled gears, worm drives, chains and treads, rubber bands and rack-and-pinion gears to 'moving to and fro', pulley systems, rubber-band power and 'making music'. Vol. 2 'Wheeled Wonders' (ix + 131 pages) covers vehicles that drive, turn, move things and reverse. Vol. 3 'Fantastic Contraptions' (161 pages) covers walkers (4-, 6- and 2-legged), wind, weights, vibration, springs, magnets, lights, pneumatics, solar panels, off-centre axis of rotation, intermittent movement and changeover mechanisms. Each book holds 'hundreds' of small working models. Sariel's Builder's Guide (2nd edition) has 25 chapters in 5 parts: Basics (concepts, pieces, studless vs studded, axles/bushes/joints, wheels), Mechanics (gears, chains and pulleys, levers and linkages, custom mechanical solutions, pneumatics, building strong), Motors (LEGO motors, Power Functions, RC), Advanced mechanics (steering, suspension, tracked vehicles, transmissions, adders and subtractors, planetary gearing, 3D-printing custom pieces) and Models (form vs function, scaling, modelling). The 1st edition had over 500 figures and 40 building instructions; the 2nd added 13 more instructions
coverage.organisation: Isogawa: by what the mechanism does or what powers it (e.g. 'Worm drives', 'Moving to and fro', 'Using magnets', 'Intermittent movement', 'Changeover mechanisms'), with pictograms instead of words; even the table of contents uses icons (ROBOTMAK3RS review). This works very well for someone who doesn't know the terms: you browse pictures by the motion you want. Sariel: a textbook order from basics to advanced, by mechanical topic (gears, linkages, pneumatics, steering, suspension, transmissions), with an index. It uses correct engineering names, so it suits readers who can name what they want
coverage.scope_match: medium. Both are catalogues of mechanism TYPES (gear trains, worm drives, differentials, planetary gearing, gearboxes, steering and suspension linkages, intermittent motion, walkers), which fits the in-scope gear trains and semi-complex mechanisms. But everything is built from one proprietary toy system, so the connection methods themselves (pins, axles, bushes) are LEGO-specific, and there is little on connections for printed, machined or woodworking parts, adhesives or special locking behaviours
coverage.taxonomy_used: No formal taxonomy. Isogawa groups models into themed sections (22 in Simple Machines, 17 in Fantastic Contraptions) by motion or power source. Sariel uses 5 parts and 25 chapters by mechanical topic (Basics, Mechanics, Motors, Advanced mechanics, Models)
coverage.example_types: Worm drive (worm gear); rack and pinion; gears at an angle (bevel gears); gears in a turntable (slewing ring drive); chain and sprocket drive; rubber-band (belt) drive; pulley system (block and tackle); differential; adders and subtractors (differential used to add or subtract two motions); planetary gearing (epicyclic gear train); sliding-gear and driving-ring gearboxes (manual transmission); virtual-pivot steering (steering linkage whose pivot sits in the tyre centre line); wheeled and tracked suspension; levers and linkages; walker linkages (four-, six- and two-legged walking mechanisms); intermittent movement (intermittent-motion mechanism); changeover mechanism (direction-dependent output switching, e.g. by reversing a motor); off-centre axis of rotation (eccentric/crank); pneumatic devices (pneumatic cylinders and valves); Sariel's 'Infinite Stepper Mechanism' (web post)
coverage.making_methods: LEGO Technic building (toy construction system), educational robotics (LEGO Mindstorms), and in Sariel's 2nd edition a chapter on 3D printing custom LEGO-compatible pieces. Principles carry over to general mechanism design, but no CNC, woodwork or general 3D-printing design rules
coverage.item_count: Isogawa: 'hundreds' of small working models per book, across 3 books (about 157 + 131 + 161 pages); exact counts not found. Sariel 2nd edition: 25 chapters, 424 pages, over 500 figures and 53 building instructions (40 in the 1st edition plus 13 new) [uncertain]
coverage.special_behaviours_covered: torque-limiting: not confirmed in the opened tables of contents (LEGO's clutch gear is a torque limiter and is likely shown, but unverified) [uncertain]; self-locking: yes, worm drives (a Simple Machines section) are the classic self-locking gear; hand-release only: no; one-way/ratchet: not confirmed [uncertain]; indexing/detent: yes, 'Intermittent movement' in Fantastic Contraptions, and Sariel's 'Infinite Stepper Mechanism'; over-centre: no evidence; compliant: only rubber bands and springs as energy stores ('Rubber band power', 'Using springs'), no flexures; print-in-place: no, although Sariel covers 3D printing custom pieces; gear trains/gearboxes: yes, the core strength (gear combinations, gears in series, worm, bevel, planetary, differentials, sliding-gear and driving-ring transmissions); powered connectors: partly (motors, Power Functions and RC systems, pneumatics, 'Using magnets', solar panels) but no electromagnetic latches or motorised locks; adhesive types: no (LEGO is built without glue)
coverage.entry_structure: Isogawa: a short title and pictograms, then close-up colour photos of each small model from several angles, with parts colour-coded so you can rebuild it from the pictures alone; no step-by-step instructions and almost no text. Sariel: textbook chapters with explanation, computer-rendered diagrams, tables (e.g. a gear ratio table) and, for selected mechanisms, step-by-step building instructions
coverage.audience_level: hobbyist (children to adult LEGO fans, schools and educational robotics). Sariel's book 'starts simple for first-time builders, but quickly move[s] to advanced material'

usefulness.beginner_friendliness: high. Isogawa's books need no reading at all: you learn each mechanism from photos and icons. Sariel's book is written plainly, 'doesn't have the feel of a school science textbook' (The Lego Car Blog) and explains gear ratios and linkages from first principles, but assumes you are building with LEGO parts
usefulness.has_images: yes, full colour throughout. Isogawa: large, close-range photos from several angles with colour-coded parts. Sariel: clear rendered diagrams (the author is a graphic designer; over 100 figures were redrawn for the 2nd edition)
usefulness.has_animations: no in the books. Both authors have YouTube channels with videos of mechanisms (Sariel is described as YouTube's most viewed LEGO Technic builder; Isogawa's channel is mentioned in publisher copy). The ROBOTMAK3RS review says No Starch hosted videos of many of the Isogawa designs [uncertain]
usefulness.gaps: Everything assumes LEGO parts, so dimensions, tolerances and joints do not carry over directly to 3D printing or machining; no plain-language index of 'what do I need this for'; nothing on snap fits, flexure design, adhesives, quick-release or hand-release locking, over-centre latches or torque limiters (as far as the tables of contents show); Isogawa has no explanations of why a mechanism works; paid and copyrighted, so pictures cannot be reused
usefulness.good_for_entry_links: no for per-mechanism links: these are books with no per-mechanism web pages. Link the whole book (e.g. https://sariel.pl/guide2/ or the Internet Archive record https://archive.org/details/simplemachines0000isog) as further reading. Sariel's blog does have stable per-mechanism posts that suit single entries, e.g. https://sariel.pl/2026/05/infinite-stepper-mechanism/ and https://sariel.pl/2026/07/2-speed-sliding-gear-transmission/ (URLs seen on sariel.pl, not opened individually) [uncertain]
usefulness.reusable_data: not reusable: printed books with no dataset or API. Tables of contents are available as library metadata (Open Library, Internet Archive), which can be read but not the content itself. The list of mechanism names is only a set of facts that can be referenced
usefulness.maintained: Books in print as of the last editions (Idea Books 2010; Builder's Guide 2nd edition 2016), with no newer editions found. LEGO parts have changed since (e.g. Power Functions and RC are now discontinued). Sariel's website is active, with new mechanism posts in May and July 2026. Isogawa has continued with newer No Starch titles up to 2021 (Non-Electric Models: Simple Machines, MINDSTORMS Robot Inventor Idea Book)
usefulness.ideas_to_borrow: (1) Pictogram-led navigation: an icon for each motion ('to and fro', 'turns 90 degrees', 'stops and starts') that lets non-readers browse, a good model for flow-chart answer buttons. (2) One idea per photo, shown from several angles with colour-coded parts, so the working principle is obvious without text. (3) Grouping by power source or effect ('using springs', 'using magnets', 'using weights', 'using vibration'). (4) Sariel's split of 'basics -> mechanics -> motors -> advanced mechanics', which suits a learning path. (5) Tables of ready-made combinations (gear-ratio table, compatible transmission parts). (6) A 'form vs function' trade-off discussion that could become a 'what to watch out for' field
usefulness.design_rules_given: Only LEGO-unit numbers: gear ratios and tooth counts, LEGO module spacing (studs), motor specs and which parts fit together (e.g. transmission-ring compatibility). No clearances, strain limits or fits for general making, except for the qualitative advice in Sariel's 3D-printing chapter [uncertain]
usefulness.generator_or_parametric: No generator in the books. Sariel offers separate web tools and Android apps (Gear Ratio Calculator, LEGO Units Converter, Model Scaler, LEGO Wheels table, LEGO Motors specs chart), linked from sariel.pl, and a July 2026 post says the source code of his tools for adult LEGO fans is now available
usefulness.file_formats: Printed paperback and ebook (an ebook edition of the 2nd edition was announced in The Lego Car Blog review; retailer listings seen only in search results) [uncertain]; Internet Archive lending copies (in-browser reader, plus DRM-protected PDF/EPUB loans). No CAD, STL or LDraw files in the books
usefulness.terminology_value: low to medium. Sariel uses correct engineering names (differential, planetary gearing, steering and suspension systems, transmissions) and defines technical terms, but mixes in LEGO jargon (studless, liftarm, driving ring). Isogawa is almost wordless. Not an authority for proper names or translations
usefulness.decision_support: None as selector logic. Isogawa's icon-coded contents let you pick by motion visually; Sariel has comparison tables (gear ratios, motor characteristics, compatible parts) and discusses pros and cons of options (e.g. planetary gearing pros and cons, studless vs studded building), but no flow chart
usefulness.derived_from_or_overlaps: The Isogawa English editions are translations/re-editions of his earlier Japanese 'Red, Blue and Green' books, and his later Power Functions and Non-Electric Models books reuse the same photo-only format. Sariel's 2nd edition updates and extends his 2012 1st edition (30-50% rewritten, per the author). Both overlap with other LEGO mechanism collections (e.g. Technicopedia, linked from sariel.pl) and, for principles, with general mechanism books such as 507 Mechanical Movements
